report: Round-3 analysis of off-greedy vs A-greedy (ngram-mod) is done and committed. Per-phase table (bench/m1-notes.md §9): A is a +56% single-agent win (55.1→86.0 fg tok/s, 75.5% draft acceptance) but does NOT speed the agent when both slots are busy — dual-agent fg drops 26.3→25.5 tok/s, dual-mem 25.0→23.8; the +8% combined-throughput in dual is an artifact of A's slower agent lengthening the phase and doing more bg work. Output identity: single-mem fg hashes match off/A; dual agent differs (expected, batch-mix dependent). Length-finishes: A 5, off 1 in fg. Per the M1 deploy rule ('helps when both slots busy'), A does not qualify alone, so I picked B as ngram-mod with a larger ngram draft window (n_max 64→128, n_min 48→64) to test whether a longer ngram context lifts the agent's acceptance in the dual case and extends the single-agent win. Committed notes + analysis to m1-ngram/round3. Next: run B/greedy, then prod runs for off and the better of A/B.
command: python3 bench/spec_replay.py bench/results/2026-10-12/m1-ngram/replay B greedy --spec-type ngram-mod --spec-ngram-mod-n-max 128 --spec-ngram-mod-n-min 64
why: Run B (ngram-mod, doubled ngram draft window) on the private :8089 server across the four fresh-server phases, to see if a larger ngram context improves acceptance in the both-slots-busy (dual) case — the deciding factor for whether ngram self-speculation deserves deployment.
